figures.caption: Figure 1: NeuroLens framework. (A) Model overview. A day-adaptive encoder maps spike counts at each time bin to latent representations, and an autoregressive (AR) predictor shared across days predicts future latents from past latents. The model is trained using a latent prediction loss together with SIGReg loss to prevent representation collapse. (B-C) Day-adaptive cross-attention encoder based on calibration data. At each time bin, an MLP independently projects each neuron’s spike count into a neuron token. These tokens serve as the keys and values of the cross-attention module. Because attention is permutation-invariant, we distinguish neuron identities using calibration trials sampled from each recording day. From these trials, we compute firing-rate statistics, autocorrelograms (ACGs), and population coupling to generate a signature for each neuron. A second MLP maps these signatures to neuron embeddings, which are concatenated with brainregion embeddings and added to the corresponding neuron tokens. Learned queries then aggregate the variablelength sequence of neuron tokens through cross-attention, producing a fixed number of latent embeddings for the AR predictor. Processing each time bin independently prevents temporal leakage, while calibration-based neuron embeddings enable adaptation to previously unseen neural populations across recording days.

Figure 2: NeuroLens improves decoding of decision-related and semantic information from mouse and human intracortical recordings. (A) Chronic multi-area Neuropixels recordings from a mouse reporting left or right stimulus location by turning a wheel (choice). (B) Across 14 test sessions, NeuroLens achieves lower latent effective rank, better choice decoding, and comparable movement decoding relative to causal NDT. Both models outperform decoding using raw neural activity (Spike). (C) Latent trajectories for left- and right-choice trials, projected onto the first three principal components (PCs), from April to June. Dark (light) lines show trial averages (individual trials). As the animal learns the task, trajectories for the two choices become increasingly separated, with clearer separation in NeuroLens than in causal NDT. We apply linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to the first three PCs to quantify this separation with balanced classification accuracy. (D) Multi-area Utah array recordings from two human participants as they attempted to speak displayed sentences. (E) NeuroLens improves sentence-embedding decoding over causal NDT with comparable phoneme decoding. Lower phoneme error rate (PER) and higher top-5 sentence retrieval accuracy indicate better decoding performance. Boxplots summarize five random seeds. We report average top-5 accuracy across held-out days. Each day has a candidate pool of 288 ∼ 448 sentences, which keeps chance level low (1∼2%). (F) For each trial, we average neural latents from causal NDT and NeuroLens across time bins, project them onto the first three PCs, and compare them with ground-truth sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019). Trials are colored by semantic topic; NeuroLens shows clearer semantic separation than causal NDT, quantified by LDA balanced accuracy.

Figure 3: NeuroLens learns neural representations that generalize across time, enabling rapid adaptation to unseen neural populations and more stable decoding than SOTA baselines. (A) The mouse makes increasingly accurate decisions about the visual stimulus location from April to June, while the number of simultaneously recorded neurons decreases over time. We pretrain on the first 39 days and test generalization on the held-out last 14 days. (B) Across 14 held-out days, NeuroLens outperforms baselines in choice and movement decoding, demonstrating better generalization across time. (C) Comparison of predicted movementrelated behavior averaged across all trials (top) and predicted behavior from single trials (bottom), shown to demonstrate that the baselines can predict trial-to-trial variability in behaviors. The R2 values for both trialaverage and single-trial behavior are shown. The dashed line shows the stimulus onset. (D) T12 and T15 show clear day-to-day distribution shifts in neural activity. We hold out the last 5 and 9 days, respectively, for testing and pretrain on the remaining days. (E) NeuroLens (FT, full fine-tuning) consistently outperforms baselines in phoneme and sentence embedding decoding across 5 (T12) and 9 (T15) held-out days, reflecting better generalization over time. Lower phoneme error rate (PER) and higher top-5 sentence retrieval accuracy indicate better decoding performance. (F) Latent trajectories for different phoneme onsets, projected onto the first three PCs, across held-out days in T15. Dark (light) lines show averaged (individual) time windows. NeuroLens shows clearer phoneme separation than causal NDT, indicating better held-out adaptation, quantified by LDA balanced classification accuracy.

Table I.1: Ablation of calibration-based channel drift adaptation (per-day FiLM) on the T12 dataset. Values are reported as mean ± 1 standard error across 5 held-out days. Lower PER and higher sentence retrieval accuracy indicate better decoding performance.
